Every §2(d) appeal eventually reaches the same argument: the cited mark lives in a crowded neighborhood, so consumers have learned to tell similar marks apart by small differences. In In re [Applicant], the applicant made that argument with [number] third‑party registrations for marks containing [shared term]. The Board was not persuaded.

## What the Board decided

The examining attorney refused registration of [APPLIED‑FOR MARK] for [goods/services] over [REGISTERED MARK] for [goods/services]. On appeal, the Board found the marks similar in overall commercial impression, the goods [legally identical / closely related], and the trade channels presumptively the same. Against that, the third‑party evidence carried little weight.

## Why the registrations didn’t carry the day

The sixth DuPont factor asks about the number and nature of similar marks in use on similar goods. In use is the operative phrase. A registration shows that someone obtained one; it doesn't show that consumers have encountered the mark in the marketplace. The Federal Circuit has said as much: third‑party registrations offered without evidence of use, or covering goods unlike those at issue, have limited probative value (In re i.am.symbolic, llc, 866 F.3d 1315 (Fed. Cir. 2017)).

## The use evidence that would have

Contrast the cases where a crowded‑field argument has worked. In Juice Generation, Inc. v. GS Enterprises LLC, 794 F.3d 1334 (Fed. Cir. 2015), and Jack Wolfskin v. New Millennium Sports, 797 F.3d 1363 (Fed. Cir. 2015), the records showed extensive third‑party use alongside the registrations — enough to show the shared element was weak and entitled to a narrow scope of protection.

## Takeaways for practitioners

1. Pair each third‑party registration with evidence of use: web pages, retail listings, packaging.
2. Prune the list. Registrations for unrelated goods, or that are dead, dilute the argument.
3. Tie the evidence to the shared term, not to the marks as wholes.
